sentences.text: The holotype skull measures 144 mm long, and the entire animal was roughly the size of a house cat.
Its forelimbs featured a vertical upper arm bone, a ball-and-socket shoulder joint, and a hand with only three fingers touching the ground.
An enlarged area on the front edge of the shoulder blade provided space for expanded muscles to pull the limbs back.
Despite being a crocodylomorph, this creature was about the size of a domestic cat.
A tall, narrow canal in the inner ear helped the animal keep its head steady while moving on land.
James Clark and colleagues first described the genus in 2004 after finding fossils at the Wucaiwan locality in Xinjiang, China.
The species name sloani honors C. Sloan, who found the specimen, and a full bone-by-bone description was published in 2022.
Unlike modern crocodiles, Junggarsuchus moved on land and had powerful jaw muscles attached to the angular bone.
The lateral surface of the angular bone shows extensive attachment sites for jaw muscles similar to those of crown crocodilians.
It possessed a linear row of holes below the lower jaw teeth and had fewer facial nerves along the snout than related species.
Researchers believe it was a carnivore that used serrated teeth to cut flesh, likely hunting small mammals, reptiles, or baby dinosaurs.
Originally, Clark and colleagues placed Junggarsuchus as a close relative to the crocodile lineage, with the type species being J. sloani.
Later studies suggested a link to Phyllodontosuchus, but this connection was weak due to poor preservation of the other fossil.
This animal lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically within the Callovian stage between 163.5 and 162.2 million years ago.
Remains are known only from the lower member of the Shishugou Formation near Wucaiwan in China.
Scientists argue whether the absence of bony armor plates is due to how the fossil was preserved or if the animal was young.
The purpose of air-filled spaces in the skull is unclear; they might have absorbed shock or resulted from sinus invasion.
The exact way the surangular and angular bones touched each other remains uncertain, ranging from short contact to significant overlap.
It is also debated whether certain skull traits define a natural group or arose from convergent evolution.
